overview.title: Premade search spaces and model ensembling
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.1 Getting the most out of your models
overview.main_topic: Why high-level search spaces transfer across tasks (KerasTuner's premade hypermodels), and the idea of ensembling: pooling the predictions of several diverse models, starting with simple averaging
overview.central_idea: Different well-performing models capture different parts of the 'truth' about the data. Averaging their predictions (an ensemble) usually beats any single model, which is why competition winners use large ensembles.
overview.importance: Ensembling is one of the most reliable ways to gain the last bits of performance. The page gives both the intuition (the blind men and the elephant) and the simplest implementation.
learning_objectives: Explain why higher-level architecture decisions generalize better than micro-decisions, and what KerasTuner's premade hypermodels provide
Explain the assumption that makes ensembling work (independently trained good models are good for different reasons)
Implement an equal-weight average of classifier predictions
prerequisites: Classifier outputs as softmax probability arrays from model.predict
Keras Applications / pretrained models and Xception-style architectures (p.304)

summary:
The page finishes the search-space discussion from p.569. Micro-decisions are specific to a model and dataset, but **higher-level decisions generalize better across tasks and datasets**: almost every image classification problem can be solved with the same kind of search-space template. KerasTuner therefore offers **premade search spaces** for broad problem categories such as image classification: add data, run the search, get a pretty good model. Examples are the hypermodels `kt.applications.HyperXception` and `kt.applications.HyperResNet`, tunable versions of Keras Applications models.

**Section 18.1.2, Model ensembling**, starts. Ensembling means pooling the predictions of a set of different models to produce better predictions. Winners of machine learning competitions, especially on Kaggle, use very large ensembles that beat any single model, however good.

Ensembling relies on an assumption: different well-performing models trained independently are likely to be good *for different reasons*. Each looks at slightly different aspects of the data and gets part of the 'truth' but not all of it. The authors use the parable of the **blind men and the elephant**: each man touches one part (the trunk, a leg) and describes the elephant as 'like a snake' or 'like a pillar or a tree'. The men are models trying to understand the manifold of the training data, each with its own assumptions (from its architecture and its random weight initialization). None gets it fully right, but together they tell a fairly accurate story.

For classification, the simplest ensemble **averages the predictions at inference time**. The code calls `predict` on four models (`model_a` … `model_d`) and computes `final_preds = 0.25 * (preds_a + preds_b + preds_c + preds_d)`. The callout says this new prediction array should be more accurate than any of the initial ones. The next page (p.571) adds a caveat: this works only when the classifiers are roughly equally good.

paragraphs.excerpt: Ensembling relies on the assumption that different well-performing models trained independently are likely
paragraphs.what_it_says: Ensembling assumes independently trained good models are good for different reasons: each sees slightly different aspects of the data and gets part of the truth. In the parable of the blind men and the elephant, each man touches one part (trunk, leg) and describes the animal as 'like a snake' or 'like a pillar or a tree'. The men are models trying to understand the manifold of the training data, each with its own assumptions (its architecture and random weight initialization). Each gets part of the truth; pooled, they give a far more accurate description. The second printed paragraph then says that for classification, the easiest way to ensemble classifiers is to average their predictions at inference time.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each model makes errors that come partly from its own inductive biases and randomness. If those errors are not perfectly correlated, averaging reduces them. The 'truth' is the true input-output relationship (the data manifold). Each model's view of it is partial and biased in its own way. Averaging softmax outputs gives a new probability distribution per sample (the average of distributions that each sum to 1 also sums to 1), and the predicted class is its argmax.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The parable shows that ensembling depends on *differences* between models, not just their individual quality. p.571 makes this explicit: 'Diversity is strength.'
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: if M models have errors with equal variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is $\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\sigma^2$. With ρ = 1 (identical models) there is no gain; with ρ = 0 the variance drops by a factor of M.

concepts.name: Model ensembling
concepts.definition: Pooling the predictions of a set of different models to produce better predictions.
concepts.intuition: Several partial witnesses together describe the elephant better than any one of them.
concepts.technical: For classifiers, average the predicted class-probability vectors: $\bar p = \frac{1}{M}\sum_m p_m$. Gains come from errors that are not perfectly correlated between members.
concepts.significance: Competition winners use very large ensembles that beat any single model.
concepts.misconception: That ensembling many copies of the same model gives large gains. Low diversity gives only tiny improvements (p.571).

concepts.name: Premade search spaces (HyperXception, HyperResNet)
concepts.definition: Ready-made KerasTuner hypermodels that are tunable versions of Keras Applications architectures.
concepts.intuition: A good recipe template where you only plug in your ingredients (data).
concepts.technical: Hypermodels in kt.applications expose architecture and training choices as hyperparameters; you pass one to a tuner instead of a custom build_model.
concepts.significance: Higher-level decisions transfer across tasks, so a single template serves most image classification problems.
concepts.misconception: That premade search spaces remove the need for validation discipline; validation overfitting still applies (p.569).

math.title: Equal-weight ensemble of four classifiers

variables.meaning: Class-probability vector predicted by model m for input x (one row of preds_m)
Number of models in the ensemble (4)

math.operations: Elementwise sum of the prediction arrays (same shape: samples × classes) multiplied by 1/M.
math.purpose: Combine the models' beliefs so that uncorrelated errors partially cancel.
math.interpretation: Each class's ensemble probability is the mean of the members' probabilities; the predicted class is $\arg\max_k \hat p_k(x)$.
math.intuition: A vote where each model casts a soft, confidence-weighted vote.
math.numerical_example: For one image with 3 classes: $p_a=(0.7,0.2,0.1)$, $p_b=(0.4,0.5,0.1)$, $p_c=(0.6,0.3,0.1)$, $p_d=(0.3,0.6,0.1)$. Sum = (2.0, 1.6, 0.4), times 0.25 = **(0.50, 0.40, 0.10)** → class 0. Two of the four models alone would have chosen class 1.

code.title: Averaging the predictions of four classifiers
code.original_code:
preds_a = model_a.predict(x_val)
preds_b = model_b.predict(x_val)
preds_c = model_c.predict(x_val)
preds_d = model_d.predict(x_val)
final_preds = 0.25 * (preds_a + preds_b + preds_c + preds_d)
code.what_it_does: Computes the predictions of four different trained models on the same inputs, then averages them elementwise to produce the ensemble's predictions.

line_explanations.explanation: Four different models compute initial predictions on x_val (callout). For a softmax classifier each result has shape (num_samples, num_classes).
Sum and multiply by 0.25 = 1/4: an equal-weight average. The callout says this new array should be more accurate than any of the initial ones.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: x_val and four trained models with the same output format. Output: final_preds, an array of averaged probabilities of the same shape.
code.algorithm: Arithmetic mean of member probability outputs.
code.theory_link: Error averaging: partially independent errors cancel, reducing variance.
pitfalls: All models must output aligned arrays (same class order and preprocessing applied to x_val).
It assumes the models are roughly equally good; one much worse model can drag the ensemble below the best member (p.571).
If x_val was used to choose ensemble members or weights, evaluate the final ensemble on a separate test set.
Averaging logits instead of probabilities gives a different (though often similar) result.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: evaluating the ensemble vs its members on held-out data
import numpy as np
models = [model_a, model_b, model_c, model_d]
preds = [m.predict(x_test) for m in models]
for name, p in zip("abcd", preds):
    print(name, np.mean(p.argmax(axis=1) == y_test))
ensemble = np.mean(preds, axis=0)
print("ensemble", np.mean(ensemble.argmax(axis=1) == y_test))

deeper.title: Why averaging helps: error decomposition
deeper.body:
Beyond the book. Let each model's prediction error have variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$. The average of $M$ models has error variance

$$\operatorname{Var}\Big(\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_m \varepsilon_m\Big) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\,\sigma^2.$$

- $\rho = 1$ (identical models): variance stays $\sigma^2$, no gain.
- $\rho = 0.5$, $M = 4$: $0.5\sigma^2 + 0.125\sigma^2 = 0.625\sigma^2$.
- $\rho = 0$, $M = 4$: $0.25\sigma^2$.

This is the mathematical form of the blind-men parable: the gain depends on how *differently* the models err, which p.571 calls diversity.

deeper.title: Mapping the parable
deeper.body:
| Parable | Machine learning |
|---|---|
| The elephant | the true structure (manifold) of the data |
| A blind man | a trained model |
| The part he touches | the aspects of the data the model's architecture and initialization lead it to use |
| 'Like a snake' | a partial, biased model of the truth |
| Interviewing them together | averaging predictions |

The mapping follows the book's text; the table format is ours.

misconceptions.claim: An ensemble is only useful if each member is weak.
misconceptions.correction: The book's assumption is about well-performing models that are good for different reasons; competition ensembles combine strong models.

misconceptions.claim: Averaging predictions requires retraining a combined model.
misconceptions.correction: Simple averaging happens at inference time on the outputs of already-trained models.

misconceptions.claim: The averaged probabilities no longer form a valid distribution.
misconceptions.correction: An average of probability vectors that each sum to 1 also sums to 1.

takeaways: Higher-level architecture decisions transfer across tasks, so KerasTuner offers premade search spaces like HyperXception and HyperResNet.
Model ensembling pools the predictions of several models; competition winners use large ensembles.
It works because independently trained good models are good for different reasons and see different parts of the 'truth'.
The simplest classifier ensemble averages predicted probabilities at inference time.

questions.question: Why does KerasTuner provide premade search spaces such as HyperResNet?
options: Because micro-decisions transfer perfectly between datasets
Because higher-level architecture decisions generalize across tasks, so one template serves a broad problem category
Because ResNet cannot be built manually in Keras
Because premade spaces avoid validation-set overfitting
questions.answer: Because higher-level architecture decisions generalize across tasks, so one template serves a broad problem category
questions.explanation: The page says higher-level decisions generalize better and image classification problems share a search-space template. Micro-decisions are task-specific, ResNet can be built manually, and validation overfitting still applies.

questions.question: Define model ensembling in one sentence.
questions.answer: Pooling together the predictions of a set of different models to produce better predictions.

questions.question: What assumption does ensembling rely on, and how does the blind-men parable illustrate it?
questions.answer: Different well-performing models trained independently are good for different reasons, each capturing part of the truth. Each blind man touches a different part of the elephant; none is fully right, but together their descriptions are accurate.
questions.explanation: The parable maps men to models, and their touch points to the assumptions from architecture and initialization.

questions.question: Three classifiers output (0.6, 0.4), (0.3, 0.7) and (0.9, 0.1) for a binary problem. What is the equal-weight ensemble prediction and the chosen class?
questions.explanation: Average each class probability across models, then take the argmax.

questions.question: According to the book, what gives each 'blind man' (model) its unique perspective?
options: Being trained on a different test set
Its unique architecture and unique random weight initialization
Using a different loss for each class
Seeing the data in a different file format
questions.answer: Its unique architecture and unique random weight initialization
questions.explanation: Stated explicitly in the parable paragraph. Test sets are never used for training, and the other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: Can you predict when averaging four models would not improve over the best one? (Check p.571.)
questions.answer: When one model is much worse than the others, or when the models are nearly identical (low diversity) so their errors don't cancel.
questions.explanation: p.571 covers both the unequal-quality caveat and the diversity requirement.
